newsitem.title: USA: BOXING-TYSON'S DAY OF RECKONING, COULD BE BANNED FOR EAR-BITING.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-TYSON'S DAY OF RECKONING, COULD BE BANNED FOR EAR-BITING.

text.p: The day of reckoning has arrived for Mike Tyson, who faces a possible ban from boxing and a nearly $3 million fine Wednesday at a disciplinary hearing to determine punishment for his biting of Evander Holyfield's ears in the ring.

Marc Ratner, executive director of the Nevada State Athletic Commission, said he thought Tyson would attend the hearing at the Las Vegas City Hall where the five-man commission will decide the fighter's fate.
"I am hoping he is there to explain to the world his actions," said Ratner. "It is his chance to have a forum."
Ratner told the Las Vegas Review-Journal that the state attorney's office was seeking a revocation of Tyson's boxing license and a $3 million fine from the disciplinary hearing.
The state complaint alleges Tyson was guilty of a foul for biting Holyfield twice and that his conduct brought discredit on boxing.

With almost everyone, from the president of the United States on down, expressing horror after Tyson was disqualified after the third round of the June 28 bout, there is pressure on the Nevada commission to come down hard on the fighter.
It was not known if Tyson was planning to attend.
Commission chairman Elias Ghanem said: "The Commission is not forcing him to come. If he wants to come, fine."
Last week, Tyson's lawyer said the fighter would attend if it was in his best interests.
One member of the commission was quoted by the Las Vegas newspaper as saying Tyson's attendance would be critical.
"It is very important. It shows sincerity, it shows a little bit of humility," said Luther Mack. "I would like to hear him say to us in his own words what happened.
"We think he has to answer these questions to the commission. He got a prepared letter and apologised," said Mack, referring to a public apology Tyson made two days after the fight.
"He has never apologised before the commission... he has never come before us and apologised to us," Mack told the Review-Journal.
If Tyson's license is revoked, he would have the right to ask the commission to lift the revocation after one year.
But the commission could refuse to grant him a new license after the year.
In that case, Tyson could not reapply for a license for another year. In the case of revocation, a boxer must wait for one year each time before reapplying.
If Tyson's license is revoked, he would be fined up to 10 percent of the gross purse for the Holyfield fight under state law. The actual purse was $29,824,600 after fees were deducted.
However, if the commission decides to merely suspend Tyson, he can be fined no more than $250,000 under state law.
Holyfield, although forgiving Tyson for the bites, has called for his opponent to be banned from boxing for at least two years.

In a TV interview before he left on a trip to South Africa, the champion said the Nevada officials have a chance to make a decision that will, "make all the fighters never, ever want to do anything like that.
"Let's get the whole game of boxing to make a pitch to be better," he pleaded.
Asked if he thought Tyson's suspension should be at least two years, he said, "yeah, that or more because you (only) fight once or twice a year usually."

Under new federal laws, a suspension in Nevada could effectively bar Tyson from fighting anywhere in the United States. The law does not force other states to honour a Nevada ban, but those states would have to justify allowing him to fight in their jurisdictions.
